heading: EXHIBIT A3

fields.label: Title
fields.text: The Basic Law of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China (Hong Kong Basic Law)
fields.html: The Basic Law of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China (Hong Kong Basic Law)

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region
fields.html: Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: The Hong Kong Basic Law serves as the constitutional framework of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. It establishes the “One Country, Two Systems” principle, preserves the common law system, and guarantees fundamental rights and freedoms. It also sets out the institutional structure of government and prescribes requirements for public office, including nationality and allegiance obligations for key officials.

heading: EXHIBIT A5

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Cap. 383 Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance
fields.html: Cap. 383 Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: The Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance (Cap. 383) incorporates into Hong Kong law the relevant provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights as applied to Hong Kong. Article 11(2)(g) protects the minimum guarantees in criminal proceedings, including the right not to be compelled to testify against oneself or to confess guilt.
fields.html: The Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance (Cap. 383) incorporates into Hong Kong law the relevant provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights as applied to Hong Kong. Article 11(2)(g) protects the minimum guarantees in criminal proceedings, including the right not to be compelled to testify against oneself or to confess guilt.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This authority is relevant because it sets out core fair trial protections recognized in Hong Kong domestic law. Article 11(2)(g) is directly relevant to concerns about coercion, compelled self-incrimination, or pressure on an accused person in criminal proceedings. It can therefore be cited to show that due process and trial fairness guarantees are protected not only under international human rights standards but also under Hong Kong’s own statutory framework.

heading: EXHIBIT A7

fields.label: Title
fields.text: The Law of the People’s Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (The Hong Kong National Security Law)
fields.html: The Law of the People’s Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (The Hong Kong National Security Law)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: The Hong Kong National Security Law establishes a legal regime criminalising acts of secession, subversion, terrorist activities, and collusion with foreign forces. The provisions are broadly framed and encompass a wide range of non-violent conduct, including forms of expression and political activity. The law further introduces expanded enforcement powers, restrictive bail conditions, and mechanisms affecting judicial independence, as well as asserting extraterritorial jurisdiction.
fields.html: The Hong Kong National Security Law establishes a legal regime criminalising acts of secession, subversion, terrorist activities, and collusion with foreign forces. The provisions are broadly framed and encompass a wide range of non-violent conduct, including forms of expression and political activity. The law further introduces expanded enforcement powers, restrictive bail conditions, and mechanisms affecting judicial independence, as well as asserting extraterritorial jurisdiction.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This law is central to establishing the legal framework through which alleged acts have been carried out. Its breadth and application to non-violent conduct, including peaceful expression, support allegations that prosecutions are not limited to legitimate security concerns but form part of a broader policy targeting a civilian population. The combination of expansive offences, restrictive procedural safeguards, and extraterritorial reach is relevant to assessing whether the conduct constitutes a widespread or systematic attack pursuant to Article 7 of the Rome Statute, and whether such acts are carried out pursuant to or in furtherance of a State policy.

heading: EXHIBIT A11

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the Law of the People’s Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region
fields.html: Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the Law of the People’s Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: The Implementation Rules for Article 43 of the Hong Kong National Security Law establish additional enforcement powers in national security investigations. These include provisions requiring individuals to comply with information requests from law enforcement authorities, including the obligation to answer questions and provide access to electronic devices and related data, such as passwords. Failure to comply with such requirements may constitute a criminal offence.

fields.label: Relevance

heading: EXHIBIT B1

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Joint Declaration on the question of Hong Kong
fields.html: Joint Declaration on the question of Hong Kong

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: The Sino-British Joint Declaration is an international treaty between the United Kingdom and the People’s Republic of China setting out the terms for the transfer of sovereignty over Hong Kong in 1997. It establishes the principle of “One Country, Two Systems,” under which Hong Kong would retain its existing legal, economic, and social systems, as well as rights and freedoms, for 50 years after the handover.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: These materials demonstrate a broader legal trend among Commonwealth jurisdictions to abolish, repeal, or suspend sedition offences. The United Kingdom abolished sedition as a criminal offence under the Coroners and Justice Act 2009. Australia repealed its federal sedition provisions through legislative reform in 2010. In India, the Supreme Court in S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022) suspended the operation of the colonial-era sedition law, recognising its potential to unjustifiably restrict freedom of expression.

In India, the Supreme Court in S.G. Vombatkere v. Union of India (2022) suspended the operation of the colonial-era sedition law, recognising its potential to unjustifiably restrict freedom of expression.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This comparative legal evidence shows that the revival and enforcement of sedition offences in Hong Kong runs counter to prevailing international and Commonwealth standards. It supports the argument that such offences are widely regarded as vague, overly broad, and incompatible with democratic values and the right to free expression. This divergence is relevant in assessing whether the use of sedition laws forms part of a broader pattern of repression and procedural violations.

heading: EXHIBIT B9

fields.label: Title
fields.text: UN calls for release of Hong Kong publisher Jimmy Lai following 20-year sentence
fields.html: UN calls for release of Hong Kong publisher Jimmy Lai following 20-year sentence

fields.label: Source
fields.text: United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk
fields.html: United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk deplored the 20-year prison sentence imposed on Jimmy Lai under Hong Kong’s national security legislation, describing it as a violation of international human rights law. He stated that Mr. Lai “is a publisher sentenced to 20 years in prison for exercising rights protected under international law,” and highlighted how the vague and overly broad provisions of the legislation have been interpreted and enforced in breach of Hong Kong’s international obligations. Türk called for the verdict to be “promptly quashed as incompatible with international law” and appealed for Mr. Lai’s immediate release on humanitarian grounds, citing his advanced age (78), health concerns, and the impact of over five years in detention. The statement also notes broader repressive trends, including the criminalisation of fundamental freedoms (expression, media freedom, association) and the use of pre-NSL conduct in establishing guilt.

The statement also notes broader repressive trends, including the criminalisation of fundamental freedoms (expression, media freedom, association) and the use of pre-NSL conduct in establishing guilt.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This recent UN statement directly supports the report by confirming international concern over the compatibility of Mr. Lai’s prosecution, conviction, and sentence with international human rights standards (including ICCPR Articles 14, 19). It reinforces the lack of effective domestic remedy (as the verdict is deemed incompatible with international law) and the humanitarian urgency of release, given prolonged detention and health deterioration. While not explicitly addressing conditions of detention (e.g., solitary confinement), it bolsters the overall inference of arbitrary and coercive treatment in national security cases, aligning with prior WGAD opinions (EXHIBITS B4–B5) and Mandela Rules concerns (EXHIBIT B6).

heading: EXHIBIT B10

fields.label: Title
fields.text:
Opinions adopted by the Working Group on Arbitrary Detention at its 105th session, 23 March–1 April 2026
Opinion No. 26/2026 concerning Owen Chow Ka-shing (Hong Kong, China)
fields.html:
Opinions adopted by the Working Group on Arbitrary Detention at its 105th session, 23 March–1 April 2026

Opinion No. 26/2026 concerning Owen Chow Ka-shing (Hong Kong, China)

fields.label: Source
fields.text: United Nations Human Rights Council Working Group on Arbitrary Detention
fields.html: United Nations Human Rights Council Working Group on Arbitrary Detention

fields.label: Document Type
fields.text: Opinion of a United Nations Human Rights Mechanism
fields.html: Opinion of a United Nations Human Rights Mechanism

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This is a formal Opinion of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention concerning Owen Chow Ka-shing, one of the pro-democracy figures prosecuted in the "Hong Kong 47" primary-election case. The Working Group found his deprivation of liberty to be arbitrary under categories I, II, III and V. It found, among other matters, that he was arrested without a warrant and without being informed of the reasons; that Article 22(3) of the National Security Law ("with a view to subverting the State power") is so vague and overbroad as to violate the principle of legality; that his detention resulted from the peaceful exercise of the rights to freedom of expression, assembly, association and political participation; and that the fair-trial violations were of such gravity as to render the detention arbitrary, including a delay of 761 days between arrest and the start of trial, prolonged solitary confinement impairing the preparation of his defence, an in-camera trial, the concentration of all designated national-security judges in a single Magistrates' Court, the removal of trial by jury by certificate of the Secretary for Justice, and the appointment of national-security judges by the Chief Executive from a list not made public together with the power to issue binding certificates as to national security and State secrets – features found incompatible with judicial independence under Article 14(1) of the ICCPR. The Working Group recorded that approximately 74 per cent of persons charged with national-security offences have been denied bail under the reverse presumption in Article 42 of the National Security Law, including 11 children, some for more than a year; observed that solitary confinement beyond 15 days may itself constitute torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; and held, applying Article 4(1) of the International Law Commission's Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts, that the People's Republic of China is responsible for the conduct of the Government of Hong Kong as a State organ.

The Working Group recorded that approximately 74 per cent of persons charged with national-security offences have been denied bail under the reverse presumption in Article 42 of the National Security Law, including 11 children, some for more than a year; observed that solitary confinement beyond 15 days may itself constitute torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; and held, applying Article 4(1) of the International Law Commission's Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts, that the People's Republic of China is responsible for the conduct of the Government of Hong Kong as a State organ.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This Opinion is an authoritative determination by a United Nations human-rights mechanism of facts directly relevant to several of the crimes alleged. It supports the imprisonment and severe deprivation of physical liberty relied upon under Article 7(1)(e), including the reverse presumption against bail, the prolonged pre-trial detention, and the systematic targeting of an identifiable political group. It supports the persecution alleged under Article 7(1)(h) through the denial of fair-trial rights, in particular the designation of national-security judges by the Chief Executive from a non-public list, the concentration of such judges, the removal of trial by jury, and the resulting absence of judicial independence – matters directly relevant to the responsibility of the designated national-security judges addressed elsewhere in this report. It further supports the torture and other inhumane acts alleged under Article 7(1)(f) and 7(1)(k), through the finding that prolonged solitary confinement may amount to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. Finally, the Working Group's application of Article 4(1) of the Articles on State Responsibility supports the attribution of the conduct of the Hong Kong authorities to the People's Republic of China and the existence of a State policy for the purposes of Article 7(2)(a). The Working Group determines the arbitrariness of detention under international human-rights law and does not make a determination of criminal responsibility for crimes against humanity; this Opinion is relied upon as authoritative evidence of the underlying facts and of their contrariety to international law.

(Hong Kong Police Fire 16,000 Tear Gas Rounds in Six Months, Deploy Forces Ahead of Citywide Strike)
fields.html:
半年發1.6萬催淚彈 港警佈防大三罷

(Hong Kong Police Fire 16,000 Tear Gas Rounds in Six Months, Deploy Forces Ahead of Citywide Strike)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report documents the Hong Kong Police Force’s response to the 2019 protests, including large-scale crowd-control operations and deployments. During the first six months of the protests, the authorities officially acknowledged the deployment of approximately 16,000 shots of tear gas and 13,900 bullets. It highlights the scale and intensity of force used in response to widespread demonstrations and strikes.

During the first six months of the protests, the authorities officially acknowledged the deployment of approximately 16,000 shots of tear gas and 13,900 bullets. It highlights the scale and intensity of force used in response to widespread demonstrations and strikes.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This report is relevant as evidence of widespread and sustained use of force by state authorities in response to civilian protests. The scale and frequency of tear gas and projectile deployment support the existence of a broader pattern of violent suppression, which may be indicative of a state policy under Article 7 of the Rome Statute. It also provides contextual support for assessing whether such conduct forms part of a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population.

It also highlights public backlash and criticism of police use of live ammunition, with concerns raised about excessive force and escalation in protest policing tactics.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official report published by the Hong Kong Department of Justice provides statistical data on conviction rates within the ordinary criminal justice system. It indicates that conviction rates in the Magistrates’ Courts were approximately 60.7% in 2023 and 60.8% in 2024, while in the Court of First Instance – where criminal cases are generally tried by a jury – the rates were 55.8% in 2023 and 58.7% in 2024.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This exhibit provides a baseline for comparison with national security prosecutions. The significantly lower conviction rates in ordinary criminal proceedings, particularly in cases involving jury trials, highlight a marked disparity when contrasted with the reported conviction rate exceeding 95% (see EXHIBIT C12) in national security cases. This disparity is relevant to assessing whether national security proceedings are subject to materially different procedural conditions, and supports concerns regarding fair trial rights, including equality of arms, judicial independence, and the presumption of innocence under international human rights law.

(Average daily remand population hits 25-year high; Six Correctional Institutions Over Capacity, Occupancy Rate Exceeds 100%)
fields.html:
日均還柙人數創25年新高 6懲教院所迫爆 收容率超100%

(Average daily remand population hits 25-year high; Six Correctional Institutions Over Capacity, Occupancy Rate Exceeds 100%)

fields.label: Source
fields.text: am730 through Yahoo News (Local & International Media Outlet)
fields.html: am730 through Yahoo News (Local & International Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report cites data released by the Hong Kong Correctional Services Department in February 2026, indicating a significant increase in both the overall prison population and the remand population in 2025. The average daily prison population reached 10,315, with the overall occupancy rate rising from 85% to 92%. Notably, the average daily remand population increased to 4,217, representing an approximate 16% rise from the previous year and marking the highest level since 2000. Among approximately 30 correctional institutions, six recorded average occupancy rates exceeding 100%, including Tung Tau Correctional Institution (146%), Stanley Prison (132%), and Tai Lam Centre for Women (125%). The report further notes that authorities have reallocated capacity across institutions to address overcrowding and have commenced partial redevelopment works at Lai Chi Kok Reception Centre. Overall, the data reflect a persistent and serious overcrowding problem within Hong Kong’s correctional facilities.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official statistical page published by the Hong Kong Correctional Services Department (CSD) provides data on the number of persons under its management, including sentenced prisoners, remand detainees, and other categories of persons in custody. The data show fluctuations and an overall upward trend in the custodial population in recent years, with a notable proportion comprising remand detainees. The statistics distinguish between different categories of persons in custody and provide insight into institutional capacity pressures and population composition within Hong Kong’s correctional system.

heading: EXHIBIT C17

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Young activists recall abuse at Hong Kong juvenile correctional facility
fields.html: Young activists recall abuse at Hong Kong juvenile correctional facility

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report documents testimonies from multiple young activists who were detained in Hong Kong juvenile correctional facilities. The former detainees describe experiencing physical violence, intimidation, and sexual abuse while in custody. According to their accounts, certain inmates–reportedly referred to as “B-boys”–were allowed or encouraged by correctional officers to target other prisoners, particularly those identified as political detainees. The report further highlights the vulnerability of minors in detention, including allegations that a 15-year-old boy was subjected to anal rape. These accounts suggest an environment in which abuse was not only prevalent but enabled through institutional tolerance or complicity.

fields.html: I was an American political prisoner in Hong Kong – and saw the savagery and squalor firsthand

fields.label: Document Type
fields.text: Opinion Published by International Media Outlet
fields.html: Opinion Published by International Media Outlet

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This opinion piece, authored by Samuel Bickett, a former detainee identifying as an American political prisoner in Hong Kong, provides a first-hand account of detention conditions. The author describes overcrowded and unsanitary facilities, harsh treatment by correctional staff, and a climate of intimidation and violence within prisons. The account further alleges that certain inmates were informally empowered by prison authorities to exert control over others, contributing to abuse and coercion. The author portrays the prison environment as degrading and punitive, particularly toward individuals detained in politically sensitive cases.

監獄修訂規則本周五刊憲即時生效　保安局稱及早防範化解國安風險
(Prisons (Amendment) Rules to Be Gazetted This Friday and Take Immediate Effect. Security Bureau Says Early Prevention Needed to Defuse National Security Risks.)
fields.html:
監獄修訂規則本周五刊憲即時生效　保安局稱及早防範化解國安風險

(Prisons (Amendment) Rules to Be Gazetted This Friday and Take Immediate Effect. Security Bureau Says Early Prevention Needed to Defuse National Security Risks.)

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Radio Television Hong Kong (RTHK), Government Media Outlet of Hong Kong
fields.html: Radio Television Hong Kong (RTHK), Government Media Outlet of Hong Kong

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report concerns amendments to Hong Kong’s Prison Rules, gazetted on 18 July 2025 and taking immediate effect. The revised rules expand the powers of correctional authorities on grounds of “national security,” including the authority to restrict or prohibit access to prisoners by certain legal representatives and religious personnel. The stated justification by the Security Bureau is the need for early prevention and mitigation of national security risks within custodial institutions. These measures introduce discretionary controls over prisoners’ access to legal counsel and spiritual support.
fields.html: This report concerns amendments to Hong Kong’s Prison Rules, gazetted on 18 July 2025 and taking immediate effect. The revised rules expand the powers of correctional authorities on grounds of “national security,” including the authority to restrict or prohibit access to prisoners by certain legal representatives and religious personnel. The stated justification by the Security Bureau is the need for early prevention and mitigation of national security risks within custodial institutions. These measures introduce discretionary controls over prisoners’ access to legal counsel and spiritual support.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the institutionalization of restrictions on fundamental safeguards within detention, particularly the right to legal representation and access to independent counsel, as well as freedom of religion. The invocation of “national security” as a basis for denying such access introduces broad and vague discretionary powers, which may be used to isolate political detainees and impede their ability to prepare a defense.
Such measures are relevant to establishing deprivation of due process and fair trial rights, as well as persecutions under Article 7 of the Rome Statute, particularly where denial of legal and external contact contributes to coercion, isolation, or abuse. When considered alongside other evidence, this supports the existence of a systematic framework enabling the control and repression of political prisoners through custodial regulations.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This exhibit is relevant as contemporaneous visual evidence of the use of potentially lethal force by law enforcement during the 2019 crackdown on protests. It supports allegations concerning excessive force against civilians and is further relevant to the subsequent absence of effective accountability measures, including failed attempts to pursue private prosecution arising from the incident. It may also assist in assessing whether patterns of force formed part of a broader attack directed against a civilian population.

heading: EXHIBIT C22

fields.label: Title
fields.text: CONSTITUTIONAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE LAW LIST NO 2270 OF 2020
fields.html: CONSTITUTIONAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE LAW LIST NO 2270 OF 2020

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This judgment of the High Court of Hong Kong concerned a judicial review challenge arising from decisions of the Secretary for Justice to intervene in and discontinue private prosecutions initiated by former lawmaker Ted Hui (Hui Chi-fung). The private prosecutions related to two 2019 protest-era incidents: the shooting of a protester by a police officer and a taxi driver allegedly driving into protesters. The Court dismissed the challenge and upheld the Secretary for Justice’s decisions to take over and terminate the prosecutions.
fields.html: This judgment of the High Court of Hong Kong concerned a judicial review challenge arising from decisions of the Secretary for Justice to intervene in and discontinue private prosecutions initiated by former lawmaker Ted Hui (Hui Chi-fung). The private prosecutions related to two 2019 protest-era incidents: the shooting of a protester by a police officer and a taxi driver allegedly driving into protesters. The Court dismissed the challenge and upheld the Secretary for Justice’s decisions to take over and terminate the prosecutions.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This exhibit is relevant to the question of whether genuine domestic accountability mechanisms existed in relation to serious allegations of violence arising from the 2019 crackdown. It evidences that attempts by private individuals to pursue criminal accountability for alleged violence against protesters were ultimately discontinued through executive intervention, with subsequent judicial review unsuccessful. It may therefore support allegations of impunity, institutional protection from prosecution, and the absence of effective domestic remedies.

fields.label: Source

fields.html: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights

fields.label: Document Type
fields.text: Submission to a United Nations Committee by Civil Society Organizations
fields.html: Submission to a United Nations Committee by Civil Society Organizations

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This is a joint submission by Hong Kong Watch, Freiheit für Hongkong e.V. and Hongkonger in Deutschland e.V. to the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, prepared in advance of the Committee’s review of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Drawing on first-hand testimony from exiled women human rights defenders and open-source material, it documents gender-based violence against women during and after the 2019 protests, including sexual assault and harassment by police officers, the case of the then 18-year-old complainant referred to publicly as Ms X, and reported sexual violence at the San Uk Ling Holding Centre.
fields.html: This is a joint submission by Hong Kong Watch, Freiheit für Hongkong e.V. and Hongkonger in Deutschland e.V. to the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, prepared in advance of the Committee’s review of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Drawing on first-hand testimony from exiled women human rights defenders and open-source material, it documents gender-based violence against women during and after the 2019 protests, including sexual assault and harassment by police officers, the case of the then 18-year-old complainant referred to publicly as Ms X, and reported sexual violence at the San Uk Ling Holding Centre.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This submission is relevant to the material element of sexual violence under Article 7(1)(g) and to the absence of genuine domestic remedies. It sets out the timeline of the Ms X case – the rape complaint of 22 October 2019, the attempted seizure of her medical records, the police characterisation of the complaint as containing “fake information”, and the subsequent decision to pursue her for “making a false statement” – and documents the reported sexual violence and forced strip searches at San Uk Ling and the absence of any investigation. It further evidences the deterrent effect on other women and the dysfunction of the complaints mechanisms, supporting the inference that sexual violence operated as an instrument of repression directed against an identifiable group.

fields.text: Open Letter Condemning Police Seizure of Medical Records (Hong Kong Public Doctors' Association - HKPDA)
fields.html: Open Letter Condemning Police Seizure of Medical Records (Hong Kong Public Doctors' Association - HKPDA)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This is an open letter from the Hong Kong Public Doctors’ Association to the Chief Executive of the Hospital Authority, expressing grave concern that patients’ medical records had been disclosed to the police, purportedly pursuant to search warrants, without the patients’ knowledge or consent. It refers to the case of Ms X, sets out the duty of doctor-patient confidentiality under the Code of Professional Conduct, and calls on the Hospital Authority to challenge such warrants, to facilitate patients’ own legal challenges, and to protect seized records.

It supports the contention that the investigative process was directed against the victim rather than the alleged perpetrators, and that institutional safeguards for patients were disregarded.

fields.text: This is the written testimony of Professor Victoria Tin-bor Hui before the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission of the United States Congress, documenting the policing of the 2019 Hong Kong protests. heading: EXHIBIT C27

fields.html: Hong Kong police violence escalates dramatically: unarmed protesters shot with live rounds

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Global Voices by Hong Kong Free Press (International & Local Media Outlet)
fields.html: Global Voices by Hong Kong Free Press (International & Local Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This is a Global Voices report, republished under a content partnership with the Hong Kong Free Press, compiling contemporaneous reporting on the escalation of police violence in Hong Kong in early November 2019. It records the shooting of an unarmed protester with live rounds at Sai Wan Ho, the death of a 22-year-old student, and the allegation of gang rape at Tsuen Wan Police Station – including that the police confirmed receiving the complaint on 22 October, that the complainant underwent an abortion on 5 November, and that DNA had been gathered from the foetus as evidence – together with the police statement of 26 October concerning the San Uk Ling Holding Centre.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This report is relevant to the Ms X case and to the absence of an effective complaints mechanism. It corroborates the preservation of DNA from the foetus as potential forensic evidence, and records that on 26 October 2019, four days after the police complaints office had been notified, a police spokesperson stated that no complaint of sexual assault had been received in respect of the San Uk Ling Holding Centre, while declining to say whether complaints had been received in respect of Tsuen Wan Police Station or other facilities. It also provides contextual evidence of the escalation of potentially lethal force during the relevant period.

fields.html: Hong Kong Free Press by Agence France-Presse (AFP) (Local & International Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This is an Agence France-Presse report, carried by Hong Kong Free Press, of the announcement on 11 December 2019 that the International Expert Panel appointed to advise the IPCC, chaired by Sir Denis O'Connor, had "taken the decision to formally stand aside from its role". The Panel stated that "a crucial shortfall was evident in the powers, capacity and independent investigative capability of IPCC", that discussions with the IPCC over the preceding month had produced no progress, and that a fully independent inquiry would be better suited to the task. The report also records that the Chief Executive and the police had repeatedly rejected calls for an independent inquiry into police conduct.

fields.label: Title
fields.text:
Submission from Hong Kong Watch to the Committee on the Rights of the Child's 103rd Pre-Sessional Working Group
Alternative Report on the People's Republic of China (Hong Kong Special Administrative Region)
fields.html:
Submission from Hong Kong Watch to the Committee on the Rights of the Child's 103rd Pre-Sessional Working Group

Alternative Report on the People's Republic of China (Hong Kong Special Administrative Region)

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Hong Kong Watch (submission to the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child)
fields.html: Hong Kong Watch (submission to the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child)

fields.label: Document Type
fields.text: Submission to a United Nations Treaty Body by a Civil Society Organisation
fields.html: Submission to a United Nations Treaty Body by a Civil Society Organisation

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This submission documents the ill-treatment of children in Hong Kong's juvenile correctional facilities, drawing substantially upon the CFHK Foundation's September 2025 report based on interviews with 17 former prisoners. It records that juvenile facilities are notorious for excessive violence, and that the Correctional Services Department (CSD) operates an inmate hierarchy in which designated orderlies (known as "B-boys") are permitted to beat, extort and sexually assault other juvenile detainees. It documents the case of a political activist imprisoned at the age of 17 who was subjected to prolonged physical and sexual violence over a three-month detention at Pik Uk Correctional Institution, including being forced to perform oral sex under threat of further violence; records that at least eight of the seventeen former prisoners interviewed had been subjected to or had witnessed severe physical abuse; and describes a further 17-year-old repeatedly assaulted by a privileged inmate while guards "turned a blind eye", who emerged with post-traumatic stress disorder. It further records the routine use of solitary confinement ("removal from association", with 879 recorded cases in 2024), the CSD's exclusive control of its own grievance process and its retaliation against those who complain, and the absence of any independent international monitoring of juvenile facilities. It records that more than 10,000 persons have been arrested on protest-related charges since 2020, including children, and that minors have been convicted and imprisoned under the National Security Law, including a 16-year-old sentenced to 42 months' imprisonment in December 2025.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This submission is relevant to the assessment of sexual violence under Article 7(1)(g), evidencing that the victims of sexual violence in custodial settings included minors, and corroborating the allegation that such violence formed part of the conduct in detention facilities. It is relied upon on the basis that the sexual and physical violence occurred through a custodial hierarchy imposed and tolerated by the Correctional Services Department, which also controlled and suppressed the mechanism through which such conduct could be reported – such that the conduct is attributable to the State through institutional design and acquiescence, rather than constituting isolated inmate misconduct. It further supports the torture and other inhumane acts alleged under Article 7(1)(f) and 7(1)(k), through the severe physical abuse of juvenile detainees and the routine use of prolonged solitary confinement, and supports the widespread character of the attack under Article 7(1) through the scale of imprisonment and the extension of prosecution and imprisonment to children. This exhibit is a civil-society submission drawing substantially upon the underlying CFHK Foundation report (see EXHIBIT C14); the submission's separate treatment of academic freedom in schools is not relied upon for the purposes of Article 7.

heading: EXHIBIT C34

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Hong Kong: Submission to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, 103rd Pre-Sessional Working Group, List of Issues
fields.html: Hong Kong: Submission to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, 103rd Pre-Sessional Working Group, List of Issues

fields.label: Document Type
fields.text: Submission to a United Nations Treaty Body by an International Human Rights Organisation
fields.html: Submission to a United Nations Treaty Body by an International Human Rights Organisation

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This submission to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child documents children's-rights violations in Hong Kong under the National Security Law and the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance. Drawing on Amnesty International's research, including its June 2025 report (ASA 17/9556/2025), it records that approximately 85 per cent of concluded national-security cases involved only legitimate expression that should not have been criminalised, that bail was denied in approximately 89 percent of national-security cases, and that the average period of pre-trial detention was 11 months. It records the arrest of a 15-year-old boy in July 2025 for membership of a Taiwan-based diaspora group and his sentence, following a guilty plea, to 42 months' imprisonment for incitement to secession, absent any evidence of violence. On conditions of detention, it records interviews conducted in 2025 with nine persons detained between 2016 and 2023 across 11 facilities (including facilities for children), who reported physical violence, prolonged solitary confinement and dangerous conditions; that violence was particularly prevalent in facilities holding those aged 14 to 20; that officers took detainees to areas not covered by closed-circuit television and administered blows by a method ("chicken wing") intended to avoid leaving visible injuries; and that a former correctional officer admitted assaulting an 18-year-old detainee by thrusting a stick into his rectum, causing permanent injury, the officer's supervisor also being prosecuted. It further records that, as of 31 August 2022, 1,754 of those arrested in connection with the 2019 protests were under 18, and 517 of those prosecuted were under 18.

It records the arrest of a 15-year-old boy in July 2025 for membership of a Taiwan-based diaspora group and his sentence, following a guilty plea, to 42 months' imprisonment for incitement to secession, absent any evidence of violence. On conditions of detention, it records interviews conducted in 2025 with nine persons detained between 2016 and 2023 across 11 facilities (including facilities for children), who reported physical violence, prolonged solitary confinement and dangerous conditions; that violence was particularly prevalent in facilities holding those aged 14 to 20; that officers took detainees to areas not covered by closed-circuit television and administered blows by a method ("chicken wing") intended to avoid leaving visible injuries; and that a former correctional officer admitted assaulting an 18-year-old detainee by thrusting a stick into his rectum, causing permanent injury, the officer's supervisor also being prosecuted. fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: Relevant to persecution under Article 7(1)(h): the finding that approximately 85 per cent of concluded national-security cases involved only legitimate expression supports the contention that the criminal process was directed at protected conduct by reason of political opinion rather than at genuine criminality. title: Hong Kong: Submission to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, 103rd Pre-Sessional Working Group, List of Issues
type: Submission to a United Nations Treaty Body by an International Human Rights Organisation
summary: This submission to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child documents children's-rights violations in Hong Kong under the National Security Law and the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance. Drawing on Amnesty International's research, including its June 2025 report (ASA 17/9556/2025), it records that approximately 85 per cent of concluded national-security cases involved only legitimate expression that should not have been criminalised, that bail was denied in approximately 89 percent of national-security cases, and that the average period of pre-trial detention was 11 months. It records the arrest of a 15-year-old boy in July 2025 for membership of a Taiwan-based diaspora group and his sentence, following a guilty plea, to 42 months' imprisonment for incitement to secession, absent any evidence of violence. On conditions of detention, it records interviews conducted in 2025 with nine persons detained between 2016 and 2023 across 11 facilities (including facilities for children), who reported physical violence, prolonged solitary confinement and dangerous conditions; that violence was particularly prevalent in facilities holding those aged 14 to 20; that officers took detainees to areas not covered by closed-circuit television and administered blows by a method ("chicken wing") intended to avoid leaving visible injuries; and that a former correctional officer admitted assaulting an 18-year-old detainee by thrusting a stick into his rectum, causing permanent injury, the officer's supervisor also being prosecuted. It further records that, as of 31 August 2022, 1,754 of those arrested in connection with the 2019 protests were under 18, and 517 of those prosecuted were under 18.

fields.html: Hong Kong Centre for Human Rights (HKCHR)

fields.label: Document Type

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This civil-society alternative report to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child documents the treatment of children in Hong Kong following the 2020 National Security Law and the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance. It records, among other matters: the misuse of Care and Protection Orders under the Protection of Children and Juveniles Ordinance (Cap. 213) to detain minors who had not been charged with any offence – including a 13-year-old held for 27 days at the Tuen Mun Children and Juvenile Home and restricted from family contact before a magistrate rejected the police application, with at least four children made subject to such orders by October 2019; the systematic use by the Department of Justice of sentence-review applications to the Court of Appeal to replace minors' non-custodial, rehabilitative sentences with custodial detention, in at least 14 cases involving minors over six years; systemic physical abuse in juvenile penal facilities, including a case at the Pik Uk Correctional Institution in which a correctional officer, in collusion with inmates, assaulted an 18-year-old remand prisoner with a wooden stick, causing a torn anus and permanent injury; mandatory "patriotic" education, "re-education" of those assessed as holding "extreme ideological views", and military-style foot drills imposed on youth in custody; and a conditional non-prosecution scheme keeping the cases of approximately 7,000 uncharged protesters in legal limbo for up to seven years, conditioned upon "rehabilitation" and mainland "exchange tours", which a legal scholar has stated lacks any legal basis.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: Relevant to imprisonment and other severe deprivation of physical liberty under Article 7(1)(e), through the misuse of a child-welfare mechanism to detain uncharged minors without trial and the coercive replacement of rehabilitative sentences with custodial detention. Relevant to torture and other inhumane acts under Article 7(1)(f) and 7(1)(k), through the physical abuse of juvenile detainees by, or with the collusion of, correctional officers, and the imposition of coercive ideological programmes. Relevant to persecution under Article 7(1)(h), through the deployment of the criminal and welfare-detention apparatus against children by reason of their political activity, and the use of prolonged prosecutorial threat to coerce ideological compliance from an identifiable group of young persons. This is a civil-society submission drawing in part upon secondary sources; the underlying court records and news reports should be exhibited directly where the primary account is relied upon.

fields.text: EXPLAINED: What is the Article 23 security law in Hong Kong?
fields.html: EXPLAINED: What is the Article 23 security law in Hong Kong?

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report explains the enactment of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance in March 2024, commonly referred to as the Basic Law Article 23 legislation. The law significantly expands the scope of national security offences, including broadening the definition of sedition and increasing the severity of penalties associated with such offences.
fields.html: This report explains the enactment of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance in March 2024, commonly referred to as the Basic Law Article 23 legislation. The law significantly expands the scope of national security offences, including broadening the definition of sedition and increasing the severity of penalties associated with such offences.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This report is relevant as evidence of the expansion and entrenchment of national security offences within Hong Kong’s legal framework. The broadening of sedition and related offences supports allegations of an increasingly repressive legal regime used to criminalise expression and dissent. It further demonstrates the institutionalisation of measures that may facilitate violations of due process and fundamental rights.

fields.text: Why Hong Kong Protesters Are Outraged by Extradition Bill
fields.html: Why Hong Kong Protesters Are Outraged by Extradition Bill

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report highlights concerns raised by members of the judiciary and legal community regarding the proposed extradition bill and the broader legal framework in Hong Kong. It notes that, both prior to and during the 2019 protests, judges and legal professionals expressed criticism of the authorities, warning that the measures could undermine judicial independence, erode legal protections, and depart from fundamental democratic principles.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This report is relevant as evidence of contemporaneous concerns expressed by judicial and legal actors regarding the erosion of rule of law safeguards. This is pertinent to assessing whether the administration of justice was conducted in a manner consistent with due process, and whether it formed part of a broader pattern of conduct under Article 7 of the Rome Statute.

fields.html: Hong Kong Free Press (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report concerns a statement by the Junior Police Officers' Association, the largest staff association of the Hong Kong Police Force, following the vandalism of the graves of the parents of pro-Beijing legislator Junius Ho in the days after the Yuen Long attack of 21 July 2019. The Association's chairman, Lam Chi-wai, described those responsible as "low lives", "cockroaches" and "not human".

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This exhibit is evidence of dehumanising language used in an official capacity by the representative body of the Force's rank-and-file officers during the 2019 protests, towards persons who the Association connected with the protest movement. The characterisation of opponents as vermin and as "not human" is probative of the discriminatory animus underlying the conduct described in Part 5 of the Factual Summary, and of a climate in which mistreatment and excessive force may be normalised.

heading: EXHIBIT D9

fields.label: Title
fields.text: The West Has Abandoned Hong Kong to Totalitarianism
fields.html: The West Has Abandoned Hong Kong to Totalitarianism

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Lord Jonathan Sumption on The New Statesman
fields.html: Lord Jonathan Sumption on The New Statesman

fields.label: Document Type
fields.text: Article Written By Former Government Officials
fields.html: Article Written By Former Government Officials

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This article was written by Lord Jonathan Sumption, a former Non-Permanent Judge of the Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal (2019–2024). In the article, Lord Sumption reflects on developments in Hong Kong’s legal system following the implementation of the National Security Law. He identifies two principal concerns: first, that the law itself is repressive; and second, that judicial decision-making may be affected even in circumstances where the law allows a degree of discretion.
Lord Sumption further raises concerns regarding potential political pressures affecting the judiciary in national security cases. He recounts a conversation with a senior judge of the Hong Kong Court of Appeal, who acknowledged the constraints faced by judges operating within the broader political context, stating: “We cannot conduct a guerilla war against the Chinese state… We are pressed by the West to uphold Western values as if we were a democracy, but what can the West offer Hong Kong except moral lectures and second passports?”
The article reflects the perspective of a former senior member of Hong Kong’s highest court and provides insight into perceived institutional and systemic pressures within the judiciary.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report covers the resignation of Lord Jonathan Sumption, a Non-Permanent Judge of the Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal, in June 2024. In explaining his decision, Lord Sumption publicly stated that Hong Kong was “becoming a totalitarian state” and expressed concerns about the erosion of political freedoms and the rule of law following the implementation of the National Security Law. The report situated his resignation within broader developments affecting Hong Kong’s legal and political environment, including increasing restrictions on dissent and changes to the judicial system.

heading: EXHIBIT D11

fields.html: HKSAR Government strongly disagrees with opinions expressed by Lord Sumption

fields.label: Source
fields.html: info.gov.hk (Hong Kong Government Press-release Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This press release issued by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) Government responds to public statements made by Lord Jonathan Sumption following his resignation from the Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal. The Government strongly rejects his characterization of Hong Kong’s legal system and political environment, asserting that the rule of law remains robust and that the judiciary continues to exercise its powers independently. The statement emphasizes that the National Security Law is applied strictly in accordance with legal principles and safeguards, and reiterates the Government’s position that judicial decisions are made free from political interference.

fields.label: Document Type
fields.text: Academic Interview with Former Government Officials
fields.html: Academic Interview with Former Government Officials

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This academic interview features Baroness Brenda Marjorie Hale, former President of the United Kingdom Supreme Court and former Non-Permanent Judge of the Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal. In the interview, she reflects on her resignation from the Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal in 2021 and discusses subsequent developments in Hong Kong’s legal system. Baroness Hale expresses concern regarding the impact of the National Security Law, stating that it has “taken over the Basic Law.” She also conveys sympathy for individuals prosecuted under the National Security Law, including media proprietor Jimmy Lai, and comments on the broader implications for rights and legal protections in Hong Kong. The interview provides a retrospective assessment from a former senior judicial figure with direct experience in Hong Kong’s highest court.

It further emphasizes that rights and freedoms are protected in accordance with the law and denies that the National Security Law undermines constitutional safeguards.

fields.label: Title
fields.text: HKSAR Government strongly objects to unfair criticisms from UN Human Rights Committee
fields.html: HKSAR Government strongly objects to unfair criticisms from UN Human Rights Committee

fields.label: Source
fields.html: info.gov.hk (Hong Kong Government Press-release Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This press release issued by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) Government responds to concluding observations made by the United Nations Human Rights Committee under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). The Government expresses strong objection to what it characterizes as “unfair criticisms,” rejecting concerns raised by the Committee regarding the National Security Law and the human rights situation in Hong Kong. The statement reiterates the Government’s position that rights and freedoms are protected in accordance with the law and asserts that the National Security Law is necessary and consistent with international standards. It also criticizes what it describes as external interference in Hong Kong’s internal affairs.

fields.html: Hong Kong court rejects media tycoon Jimmy Lai’s bid to challenge foreign lawyer ban at top court

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Hong Kong Free Press (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)
fields.html: Hong Kong Free Press (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report covers a decision by the Hong Kong Court of Appeal rejecting an application by media proprietor Jimmy Lai to challenge restrictions on the admission of foreign counsel in national security proceedings. The case concerned Lai’s attempt to engage overseas legal representation in his defence, which had been opposed by the authorities on national security grounds. The court’s decision follows earlier interventions by the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress (NPCSC), which issued an interpretation of the National Security Law addressing the participation of foreign lawyers in such cases. As a result, the ability of defendants in national security cases to instruct overseas counsel is subject to additional restrictions and approval mechanisms.

(Jimmy Lai Case | Prosecution Says Articles Were Seditious; Lai Attempts to Respond, Judge Repeatedly Interrupts: “No Political Statements Will Be Allowed”)
fields.html:
【黎智英案】控方指文章煽動　黎欲反駁　法官再三打斷：不容政治言論

(Jimmy Lai Case | Prosecution Says Articles Were Seditious; Lai Attempts to Respond, Judge Repeatedly Interrupts: “No Political Statements Will Be Allowed”)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This report describes courtroom exchanges during the trial of media proprietor Jimmy Lai under the National Security Law. According to the report, while giving evidence, Lai was repeatedly interrupted by the presiding judges when attempting to explain the context and intent behind his published writings. The court restricted his responses and directed him to confine his answers, at times limiting him to answer only “agree” or “disagree”. The judges also indicated that “political statements” would not be permitted during his testimony.
The report suggests that Lai sought to explain his state of mind and the background to his statements–issues directly relevant to the prosecution’s allegations of intent and incitement–but was prevented from elaborating. The prosecution, meanwhile, was permitted to advance its interpretation of his motives and conduct.

fields.text: Family Alarmed over Jimmy Lai’s Deteriorating Health as He Languishes in Solitary Confinement in Hong Kong
fields.html: Family Alarmed over Jimmy Lai’s Deteriorating Health as He Languishes in Solitary Confinement in Hong Kong

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report describes concerns raised by the family of media proprietor Jimmy Lai regarding his physical condition while in custody in Hong Kong. According to the report, Lai has been held in conditions of prolonged solitary confinement prior to the conclusion of legal proceedings. His family reported significant deterioration in his health, including substantial weight loss and visible physical decline. Allegations cited in the report include worsening dental condition and other symptoms affecting his overall well-being. The report situated these concerns within broader scrutiny of detention conditions for individuals held under the National Security Law.

fields.label: Title
fields.text:
蘋果案｜黎智英及親友未交任何求情信 辯方指懲教署稱黎獄中體重上升資料有誤
(Apple Daily Case | Jimmy Lai and Relatives Submit No Mitigation Letters. Defense Says Correctional Services’ Claim of Weight Gain in Prison Is Incorrect)
fields.html:
蘋果案｜黎智英及親友未交任何求情信 辯方指懲教署稱黎獄中體重上升資料有誤

(Apple Daily Case | Jimmy Lai and Relatives Submit No Mitigation Letters. Defense Says Correctional Services’ Claim of Weight Gain in Prison Is Incorrect)

fields.label: Source
fields.text: 追光者 PULSE HK (Hong Kong Diaspora Media Outlet)
fields.html: 追光者 PULSE HK (Hong Kong Diaspora Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This report describes exchanges during court proceedings in the trial of Jimmy Lai, focusing on disputes regarding his physical condition in custody and the treatment of related submissions by the defence. According to the report, defence counsel raised concerns about Lai’s visible weight loss during his detention, noting a significant physical decline observable in court. This was raised in response to claims by the Correctional Services Department that Lai had gained approximately 6 kilograms during his time in custody. The prosecution, in turn, asserted that any weight change was minimal (approximately 0.8 kilograms) and described his condition as unremarkable.
The report further details the court’s response to defence submissions regarding Lai’s health and conditions of detention. It states that the judges dismissed concerns relating to his health and solitary confinement. In the course of these exchanges, the report attributes several remarks to the bench, including comments suggesting that Lai’s medical conditions were common among elderly individuals, and that weight loss “could be a good thing or a bad thing,” with an observation that some individuals might wish to lose weight. The report also states that the court expressed confidence in the prosecution’s account of Lai’s condition.
With respect to solitary confinement, the defence argued that such conditions imposed additional hardship and affected Lai’s well-being, including claims that he was asked to sign documents without full opportunity to review them. The report indicates that the court questioned whether the conditions amounted to hardship, with an analogy drawn comparing the situation to choosing between different types of hotel accommodation. While acknowledging that solitary confinement could limit social interaction, the court was reported as taking the view that it did not constitute additional punishment.

heading: EXHIBIT E10

fields.label: Title
fields.text: HKSAR v LAI CHEE YING 1st Defendant (D1), APPLE DAILY LIMITED 2nd Defendant (D2), APPLE DAILY PRINTING LIMITED 3rd Defendant (D3) & AD INTERNET LIMITED 4th Defendant (D4) – Reasons for Verdict and Reasons for Sentence
fields.html: HKSAR v LAI CHEE YING 1st Defendant (D1), APPLE DAILY LIMITED 2nd Defendant (D2), APPLE DAILY PRINTING LIMITED 3rd Defendant (D3) & AD INTERNET LIMITED 4th Defendant (D4) – Reasons for Verdict and Reasons for Sentence

fields.label: Reference Number
fields.text:
(REASONS FOR VERDICT) HCCC 51/2022 [2025] HKCFI 6291
(REASONS FOR SENTENCE) HCCC 51/2022 [2026] HKCFI 854
fields.html:
(REASONS FOR VERDICT) HCCC 51/2022 [2025] HKCFI 6291

(REASONS FOR SENTENCE) HCCC 51/2022 [2026] HKCFI 854

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This judgment concerns proceedings against Jimmy Lai under the National Security Law. The court examined, inter alia, Lai’s interactions with foreign political figures prior to the promulgation of the National Security Law, including meetings with United States politicians and public advocacy concerning the human rights situation in Hong Kong.
In its reasoning, the court found that Lai’s conduct, including his public statements and engagement with foreign actors, could amount to a form of “collusion with foreign forces.” The court interpreted certain expressions of criticism of the National Security Law and calls for international attention as implicitly amounting to requests for sanctions or hostile actions.
At the same time, the judgment indicates that there was no evidence of financial transactions between Lai and foreign political actors or media organizations. The court emphasized that the conviction was not based on the mere holding of political opinions, but rather on what it characterized as the act of putting such views “into action.”
The judgment does not address or provide relief in relation to Lai’s conditions of detention, including issues concerning solitary confinement or his physical well-being.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This document is directly relevant as it provides the court’s reasoning in applying the offence of “collusion with foreign forces,” including the interpretation of political speech, international advocacy, and engagement with foreign actors. The court’s approach to construing criticism and calls for international attention as implicit requests for sanctions may be pertinent to assessing the scope and foreseeability of the offence.
In the context of international human rights law, this evidence is relevant to the assessment of freedom of expression and fair trial guarantees under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, including Articles 14 and 19. The distinction drawn by the court between holding opinions and “putting them into action” may be examined in light of whether the conduct in question falls within protected expression or lawful advocacy.
The absence of findings or remedies concerning detention conditions may also be relevant when considered alongside evidence relating to prolonged detention and alleged deterioration in health (see EXHIBITS E7–E9), particularly in assessing whether the proceedings adequately engaged with issues affecting the defendant’s treatment and well-being.

title: HKSAR v LAI CHEE YING 1st Defendant (D1), APPLE DAILY LIMITED 2nd Defendant (D2), APPLE DAILY PRINTING LIMITED 3rd Defendant (D3) & AD INTERNET LIMITED 4th Defendant (D4) – Reasons for Verdict and Reasons for Sentence
summary:
This judgment concerns proceedings against Jimmy Lai under the National Security Law. The court examined, inter alia, Lai’s interactions with foreign political figures prior to the promulgation of the National Security Law, including meetings with United States politicians and public advocacy concerning the human rights situation in Hong Kong.
In its reasoning, the court found that Lai’s conduct, including his public statements and engagement with foreign actors, could amount to a form of “collusion with foreign forces.” The court interpreted certain expressions of criticism of the National Security Law and calls for international attention as implicitly amounting to requests for sanctions or hostile actions.
At the same time, the judgment indicates that there was no evidence of financial transactions between Lai and foreign political actors or media organizations. The court emphasized that the conviction was not based on the mere holding of political opinions, but rather on what it characterized as the act of putting such views “into action.”
The judgment does not address or provide relief in relation to Lai’s conditions of detention, including issues concerning solitary confinement or his physical well-being.

heading: EXHIBIT E11

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Justice upheld in Court of First Instance's sentence regarding Lai Chee-ying case
fields.html: Justice upheld in Court of First Instance's sentence regarding Lai Chee-ying case

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This exhibit covers public statements made by the Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, John Lee Ka-chiu, following the sentencing of Jimmy Lai to 20 years’ imprisonment by the High Court of Hong Kong. According to the exhibit, the Chief Executive described the offences as extremely serious and stated that the sentence was “deeply gratifying to the public.”
The exhibit further refers to statements by a government spokesperson who characterized Lai as the “mastermind” of the offences and asserted that the severity of the sentence was justified, including allegations of collusion with foreign forces. These statements were made in close temporal proximity to the sentencing decision and reflect the official position of the executive authorities regarding both the conviction and the punishment imposed.
The exhibit also addresses the Government’s response to concerns regarding Lai’s detention conditions. A spokesperson denied that Lai was subject to solitary confinement, describing the arrangement instead as a cessation of association with other inmates, allegedly implemented in accordance with applicable procedures and with consideration of relevant factors, including the detainee’s preferences. The Government further asserted that detention conditions remained safe, humane, and consistent with applicable standards.

These statements were made in close temporal proximity to the sentencing decision and reflect the official position of the executive authorities regarding both the conviction and the punishment imposed.

The exhibit also addresses the Government’s response to concerns regarding Lai’s detention conditions. A spokesperson denied that Lai was subject to solitary confinement, describing the arrangement instead as a cessation of association with other inmates, allegedly implemented in accordance with applicable procedures and with consideration of relevant factors, including the detainee’s preferences. The Government further asserted that detention conditions remained safe, humane, and consistent with applicable standards.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This document is relevant as it evidences statements made at the highest level of the executive immediately following sentencing in a politically sensitive case. The characterization of the sentence as “deeply gratifying to the public,” together with strongly condemnatory language directed at the defendant, may be pertinent to assessing the broader environment in which judicial proceedings take place.
In the context of international human rights law, such statements may be relevant to evaluating the appearance of judicial independence and the separation between the executive and the judiciary under Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Public endorsement of the severity of a sentence by senior officials may raise concerns regarding whether the administration of justice is perceived as independent and impartial.
The document is also relevant to assessing competing accounts regarding detention conditions. While the Government asserts that the defendant’s conditions do not constitute solitary confinement and are consistent with legal standards, this position may be contrasted with other evidence (see EXHIBITS E7–E9) indicating prolonged isolation and deterioration in health. This divergence is pertinent to evaluating whether detention conditions meet international standards, including those reflected in the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules).
Finally, insofar as the Government attributes aspects of the detention regime to the detainee’s own preferences, this raises issues regarding the validity of consent in custodial settings. In legal analysis, it may be relevant to consider whether any such consent was freely given, and whether it can justify continued conditions of prolonged isolation, particularly in light of the foreseeable and cumulative impact on physical and mental health.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
The High Court judgment in HCCC 69/2022 ([2024] HKCFI 1468) concerns the prosecution of 47 pro-democracy activists under the Hong Kong National Security Law (HKNSL) for “conspiracy to commit subversion.” The defendants participated in an unofficial primary election in July 2020 aimed at coordinating electoral strategy to obtain a legislative majority in the Legislative Council (LegCo).
The prosecution argued that, if elected, the defendants intended to use their constitutional power to veto government budgets indiscriminately, thereby forcing the resignation of the Chief Executive under the Basic Law. The Court accepted that this coordinated plan constituted a conspiracy to subvert state power under the HKNSL, even though the conduct involved participation in electoral processes and the prospective use of legislative powers.

The prosecution argued that, if elected, the defendants intended to use their constitutional power to veto government budgets indiscriminately, thereby forcing the resignation of the Chief Executive under the Basic Law. The Court accepted that this coordinated plan constituted a conspiracy to subvert state power under the HKNSL, even though the conduct involved participation in electoral processes and the prospective use of legislative powers.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the criminalization of ordinary political participation and opposition activity under the HKNSL. It shows that actions such as organizing or participating in primary elections, and planning to exercise legislative veto powers expressly provided under the Basic Law, were recharacterized as threats to national security.
The judgment illustrates how broadly defined “subversion” offenses are used to prosecute peaceful political coordination, thereby depriving individuals of their rights to political participation and due process. It further evidences the use of judicial mechanisms to legitimize politically motivated prosecutions, supporting the argument that the legal system is being instrumentalized to suppress dissent in a systematic manner.

heading: EXHIBIT E13

fields.label: Title
fields.text: AP PHOTOS: Hong Kong’s June 4 candlelit vigil over the years
fields.html: AP PHOTOS: Hong Kong’s June 4 candlelit vigil over the years

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This report documents the long-standing annual June 4 candlelight vigil in Hong Kong, organized by the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China since 1989. The vigil, held at Victoria Park, commemorated the victims of the Tiananmen Square Massacre and consistently drew thousands of participants each year.
The report highlights the significance of the event as a peaceful public assembly and a symbol of collective remembrance and political expression in Hong Kong. It also notes the broader context in which such commemorative activities have come under increasing restriction, with the Hong Kong Alliance and its members later charged under the Hong Kong National Security Law.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the suppression of peaceful assembly and collective remembrance activities under the HKNSL. It shows that long-standing, non-violent commemorative events–previously tolerated for decades–have been curtailed and criminalized following the introduction of national security legislation.
The inclusion of charges against the Hong Kong Alliance further illustrates how civil society organizations engaged in symbolic and historical expression are targeted under broadly defined national security offenses. This supports the argument that the legal framework is being used to dismantle organized civil society and restrict fundamental freedoms, including freedom of assembly and expression, in a systematic manner.

heading: EXHIBIT E14

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Hong Kong begins national security trial of Tiananmen vigil group
fields.html: Hong Kong begins national security trial of Tiananmen vigil group

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This report covers the commencement of the national security trial against key members of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China. Prominent defendants, including Lee Cheuk-yan, Albert Ho, and Chow Hang-tung, were charged with “inciting subversion of state power” under the Hong Kong National Security Law.
The report highlights that the defendants had been held in pre-trial detention for over 1,500 days after being repeatedly denied bail. The prosecution argued that the group’s advocacy for “ending one-party rule” constituted incitement to subvert state power, on the basis that one-party rule by the Chinese Communist Party is embedded in the Chinese constitutional framework.

The prosecution argued that the group’s advocacy for “ending one-party rule” constituted incitement to subvert state power, on the basis that one-party rule by the Chinese Communist Party is embedded in the Chinese constitutional framework.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the criminalization of political speech and advocacy under the HKNSL, particularly expressions calling for democratic reform. It shows that peaceful political slogans – such as “ending one-party rule” – are recharacterized as threats to national security, thereby expanding the scope of criminal liability to include core political expression.
The prolonged pre-trial detention of the defendants, exceeding 1,500 days, further evidences serious due process concerns, including the denial of bail and the use of extended detention as a punitive measure prior to conviction.
Together, these elements support the argument that the legal system is being used to systematically suppress political opposition and civil society leadership, reinforcing patterns of persecution and deprivation of fundamental rights relevant to the ICC’s assessment.

heading: EXHIBIT E15

fields.label: Title
fields.text: HKSAR v Chow Hang Tung (鄒幸彤) D1, Tang Ngok Kwan (鄧岳君) D2, Tsui Hon Kwong (徐漢光) D5 – Verdict
fields.html: HKSAR v Chow Hang Tung (鄒幸彤) D1, Tang Ngok Kwan (鄧岳君) D2, Tsui Hon Kwong (徐漢光) D5 – Verdict

fields.label: Source
fields.text: West Kowloon Magistrates' Court of Hong Kong
fields.html: West Kowloon Magistrates' Court of Hong Kong

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This judgment concerns the prosecution of Chow Hang-tung, Tang Ngok-kwan, and Tsui Hon-kwong, members of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, for failing to comply with a police notice requiring the disclosure of organizational information under the Implementation Rules of the Hong Kong National Security Law (HKNSL).
The Magistrates' Court convicted the three defendants, holding that the prosecution was not required to establish that the Hong Kong Alliance was in fact a "foreign agent." Instead, the Court accepted that the police could act on reasonable grounds to believe that the organization qualified as such. The Court considered the relatively low evidentiary threshold justified by the need for effective prevention and investigation of national security offences.
The Court also permitted the redaction of portions of the police investigation materials on public interest immunity grounds, concluding that the restricted disclosure would not undermine the defendants' right to a fair trial.
fields.html:
This judgment concerns the prosecution of Chow Hang-tung, Tang Ngok-kwan, and Tsui Hon-kwong, members of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, for failing to comply with a police notice requiring the disclosure of organizational information under the Implementation Rules of the Hong Kong National Security Law (HKNSL).

The Magistrates' Court convicted the three defendants, holding that the prosecution was not required to establish that the Hong Kong Alliance was in fact a "foreign agent." Instead, the Court accepted that the police could act on reasonable grounds to believe that the organization qualified as such. The Court considered the relatively low evidentiary threshold justified by the need for effective prevention and investigation of national security offences.

The Court also permitted the redaction of portions of the police investigation materials on public interest immunity grounds, concluding that the restricted disclosure would not undermine the defendants' right to a fair trial.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit provides direct judicial evidence of how the national security enforcement framework was interpreted and applied by the Magistrates' Court in 2023. By treating proof of actual "foreign agent" status as unnecessary for conviction, the Court adopted an interpretation that reduced the prosecution's evidentiary burden and expanded the practical scope of police information-gathering powers.
The Court's acceptance of restricted disclosure of investigative materials further illustrates the procedural disadvantages faced by defendants challenging national security investigations. These findings raise concerns regarding the presumption of innocence, access to evidence, and the ability of defendants to contest the factual basis of coercive state measures.
The judgment therefore documents an instance in which the lower court prioritized the operational effectiveness of national security enforcement over procedural protections asserted by civil society defendants. It is relevant to assessing how judicial proceedings could facilitate the exercise of coercive state powers against civil society organizations.
