fields.text: HKSAR v Chow Hang Tung (鄒幸彤) D1, Tang Ngok Kwan (鄧岳君) D2 & Tsui Hon Kwong (徐漢光) D5 – Reasons for Sentence
fields.html: HKSAR v Chow Hang Tung (鄒幸彤) D1, Tang Ngok Kwan (鄧岳君) D2 & Tsui Hon Kwong (徐漢光) D5 – Reasons for Sentence

fields.label: Source
fields.text: West Kowloon Magistrates' Court of Hong Kong
fields.html: West Kowloon Magistrates' Court of Hong Kong

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This document sets out the sentencing reasons following the convictions of Chow Hang-tung, Tang Ngok-kwan, and Tsui Hon-kwong for failing to comply with a police notice requiring organizational information under the Hong Kong National Security Law framework.
The Court sentenced each defendant to four and a half months' imprisonment, against a statutory maximum of six months. In explaining the sentences, the Court emphasized that punishment for national security-related offences must reflect the law's objective of safeguarding national security and send a clear message that violations would not be tolerated.
The Court explicitly stated that sentencing should be "punitive and sufficiently deterrent" and considered immediate imprisonment generally inevitable. It regarded the defendants' public announcement of their refusal to comply with the police notice as evidence of deliberate non-compliance. The Court also rejected Chow Hang-tung's political rationale as a basis for mitigating her sentence.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit provides direct judicial evidence of the punitive and deterrent considerations applied in sentencing civil society members prosecuted under the national security enforcement framework.
The Court's emphasis on sending a clear message to society demonstrates how sentencing was expressly linked to reinforcing compliance with national security measures. Its conclusion that immediate imprisonment was generally inevitable, together with its rejection of political justifications for non-compliance as mitigating considerations, illustrates the weight given to deterrence and enforcement objectives.
The sentencing reasons are therefore relevant to examining how criminal punishment was used to discourage resistance to national security information demands and how judicial sentencing could reinforce pressure on civil society actors.
Within a broader assessment of alleged systematic repression, this exhibit helps document the punitive consequences imposed on individuals who challenged state demands for organizational information. It complements EXHIBIT E15, which addresses the legal and evidentiary reasoning underlying the original convictions.

heading: EXHIBIT E17

fields.label: Title
fields.text: HKSAR v Best Pencil (Hong Kong) Limited (D1), CHUNG Pui-kuen (D2) & LAM Shiu-tung (D3) – Reasons for Verdict
fields.html: HKSAR v Best Pencil (Hong Kong) Limited (D1), CHUNG Pui-kuen (D2) & LAM Shiu-tung (D3) – Reasons for Verdict

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
The judgment in HKSAR v Best Pencil, et al. (29 August 2024) concerns the prosecution of Chung Pui-kuen and Patrick Lam, former editors of the now-defunct online media outlet Stand News. The defendants were convicted in relation to articles published by the outlet, including interviews with and commentaries by pro-democracy figures.
The Court held that the prosecution was not required to prove that the defendants intended to incite violence or even to cause disaffection against the government. The publications themselves were deemed sufficient to establish liability under the applicable offense, leading to punishment.
fields.html:

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the criminalization of journalistic activity and the suppression of press freedom under Hong Kong’s national security framework. It shows that media professionals can be held criminally liable for publishing or facilitating political discourse, even in the absence of intent to incite violence or disorder.
The Court’s position that intent to incite violence or disaffection need not be proven represents a significant lowering of mens rea requirements, undermining fundamental criminal law principles and expanding the scope of liability to encompass ordinary journalistic functions.
This supports the argument that legal mechanisms are being systematically used to silence independent media and restrict freedom of expression. It further evidences the broader pattern of repression targeting not only political actors but also those who report on or give voice to dissent, which is relevant to the ICC’s assessment of persecution and deprivation of fundamental rights.

heading: EXHIBIT E18

fields.label: Title
fields.text: HKSAR v LAI Man-ling (D1), YEUNG Yat-yee Melody (D2), NG Hau-yi Sidney (D3), CHAN Yuen-sum Samuel (D4) & FONG Tsz-ho (D5) – Reasons for Verdict
fields.html: HKSAR v LAI Man-ling (D1), YEUNG Yat-yee Melody (D2), NG Hau-yi Sidney (D3), CHAN Yuen-sum Samuel (D4) & FONG Tsz-ho (D5) – Reasons for Verdict

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
The judgment in HKSAR v LAI Man-ling, et al. concerns the prosecution of five speech therapists for producing and distributing a series of illustrated children’s books. The books used allegorical storytelling–depicting sheep defending their village from wolves–to portray events related to the 2019 pro-democracy protests.
The Court found that the publications constituted seditious material and concluded that seditious intent could be inferred not only from the textual content but also from the subjective interpretation of the materials. The defendants were convicted and sentenced to imprisonment on this basis.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the expansive interpretation of “sedition” offenses to encompass creative and educational materials, including children’s literature. It shows that symbolic or allegorical expression can be criminalized, even where no direct incitement to violence is present.
The Court’s approach–inferring intent beyond the text itself–illustrates a significant lowering of evidentiary thresholds and broad discretionary power in determining criminal liability. This undermines legal certainty and chills freedom of expression, particularly in educational and cultural contexts.
The prosecution of non-political professionals, such as speech therapists, further indicates that repression extends beyond traditional political actors to ordinary members of civil society. This supports the argument that the legal framework is being used systematically to suppress dissent across multiple sectors, contributing to patterns of persecution relevant to the ICC’s assessment.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
The case summary of HKSAR v Yuen Ching-ting (WKCC 2602/2023; [2023] HKMagC 13) concerns the conviction and sentencing of Yuen Ching-ting, a 23-year-old student, for publishing online messages deemed seditious. The defendant was arrested upon returning to Hong Kong from Japan, in relation to 13 posts made on Facebook and Instagram between 2018 and 2023.
The court acknowledged that the posts consisted of slogans that did not contain radical language or provoke significant public reaction, and that the defendant’s social media accounts had a relatively limited audience. She pleaded guilty; the Court treated her failure to delete the posts after the HKNSL came into force as part of her culpability.
fields.html:
The case summary of HKSAR v Yuen Ching-ting (WKCC 2602/2023; [2023] HKMagC 13) concerns the conviction and sentencing of Yuen Ching-ting, a 23-year-old student, for publishing online messages deemed seditious. The defendant was arrested upon returning to Hong Kong from Japan, in relation to 13 posts made on Facebook and Instagram between 2018 and 2023.

The court acknowledged that the posts consisted of slogans that did not contain radical language or provoke significant public reaction, and that the defendant’s social media accounts had a relatively limited audience. She pleaded guilty; the Court treated her failure to delete the posts after the HKNSL came into force as part of her culpability.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the retroactive and expansive application of national security and sedition laws to ordinary individuals engaging in low-impact online expression. It shows that even non-violent, non-inciting content with minimal audience reach can result in criminal liability.
The treatment of a failure to delete past online content as part of the defendant's culpability highlights the imposition of ongoing legal obligations on individuals for prior expression, raising serious concerns regarding legality and foreseeability.
This case further illustrates that enforcement is not limited to prominent activists or organizations but extends to ordinary citizens, including students, thereby evidencing the widespread and systematic nature of repression. It supports the argument that fundamental freedoms–particularly freedom of expression–are being severely curtailed through the use of criminal law, relevant to the ICC’s assessment of persecution and deprivation of fundamental rights.

heading: EXHIBIT E20

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Hong Kongers who clapped in court jailed on sedition charges
fields.html: Hong Kongers who clapped in court jailed on sedition charges

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This report details the conviction of Garry Pang Moon-yuen, a Christian pastor, who was prosecuted for acts conducted inside a courtroom during proceedings related to the banned June 4 candlelight vigil.
The defendant was found guilty of sedition after clapping in support of the accused during the trial. The act, though non-violent and symbolic, was treated by authorities as a criminal offense under sedition laws, resulting in imprisonment.
fields.html:

The defendant was found guilty of sedition after clapping in support of the accused during the trial. The act, though non-violent and symbolic, was treated by authorities as a criminal offense under sedition laws, resulting in imprisonment.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the criminalization of minimal, non-violent expressions of support within judicial settings. It shows that even symbolic gestures–such as clapping in a courtroom–can be construed as seditious conduct, significantly expanding the scope of criminal liability.
The case highlights the extent to which freedom of expression is restricted, including within courtrooms where public participation is ordinarily protected. It further illustrates the use of sedition laws to penalize expressions of solidarity with defendants, contributing to a chilling effect on public engagement with judicial processes.
This supports the argument that repression extends beyond formal political activity to encompass everyday acts of expression, reinforcing patterns of systematic suppression of dissent relevant to the ICC’s assessment.

heading: EXHIBIT E21

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Hong Kong university removes Tiananmen massacre statue
fields.html: Hong Kong university removes Tiananmen massacre statue

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This report covers the removal of the “Pillar of Shame,” a sculpture created by Jens Galschiøt commemorating the victims of the 1989 Tiananmen Square Massacre. The statue had been displayed at The University of Hong Kong since June 1997, symbolizing public remembrance of the event.
Despite its long-standing presence, the sculpture was removed by the university authorities. The report notes that this occurred even though the artist had offered to retrieve and relocate the work, highlighting the abrupt and controversial nature of its removal.

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Hong Kong deports mainland Chinese student after she served 6-months jail over plan to display Tiananmen banner
fields.html: Hong Kong deports mainland Chinese student after she served 6-months jail over plan to display Tiananmen banner

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Hong Kong Free Press (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)
fields.html: Hong Kong Free Press (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text:
This report details the case of Zeng Yuxuan, a mainland Chinese student who was arrested and prosecuted for planning to display a banner commemorating the Tiananmen Square Massacre. The planned banner referenced the “Pillar of Shame,” a well-known memorial symbol.
Although the act was never carried out, the defendant was convicted and sentenced to six months’ imprisonment in September 2023. Following completion of her sentence, she was deported from Hong Kong to mainland China.

summary: This report covers the conviction of veteran activist Koo Sze-yiu, who, despite suffering from terminal cancer and being in his mid-70s, was imprisoned for planning a symbolic protest using a coffin with political slogans.
relevance: This exhibit highlights the deprivation of freedom of expression affecting vulnerable and elderly individuals, demonstrating the severity of enforcement of sedition laws against non-violent political acts.

heading: EXHIBIT E24

fields.label: Title
fields.text: ‘I already miss Hong Kong’: Democracy activist Tony Chung flees to the UK
fields.html: ‘I already miss Hong Kong’: Democracy activist Tony Chung flees to the UK

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report details the case of pro-democracy activist Tony Chung, who was arrested under the charge of “secession” pursuant to the Hong Kong National Security Law at the age of 19. Following his release in June 2023 from prison, Chung was subjected to restrictive conditions, including prohibitions on speaking publicly about his conviction and on expressing or disseminating any content that could be perceived as supporting or promoting acts deemed to endanger national security. The report further notes that, due to these ongoing constraints and fears of re-arrest, Chung fled Hong Kong and sought refuge in the United Kingdom.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This exhibit demonstrates the continuing coercive control exercised over political prisoners even after release, including severe restrictions on freedom of expression. It is relevant to establishing a pattern of post-detention repression and intimidation, which extends punitive measures beyond imprisonment. Such restrictions support the argument that individuals convicted under the National Security Law remain subject to ongoing persecution on political grounds, contributing to a broader framework of systematic suppression of dissent. This evidence is pertinent to the characterization of such conduct as persecution under Article 7 of the Rome Statute, particularly when considered alongside other cases involving similar post-release constraints and forced exile.

heading: EXHIBIT E25

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Hong Kong activist flees to UK citing ‘stringent surveillance’ by national security police following his prison release
fields.html: Hong Kong activist flees to UK citing ‘stringent surveillance’ by national security police following his prison release

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report details the post-release conditions imposed on pro-democracy activist Tony Chung following his imprisonment under the Hong Kong National Security Law. After his release, Chung remained subject to stringent surveillance by national security police. He was required to attend regular reporting sessions every few weeks, during which authorities interrogated him extensively about his daily activities, personal associations, and private communications. He was also unable to take up employment without prior approval from authorities. The report further indicates that, in light of his financial hardship, authorities offered him monetary incentives to act as an informant. Facing continued monitoring and coercion, Chung ultimately fled Hong Kong and sought asylum in the United Kingdom.

23條首執行 國安囚犯未提早獲釋 倘按過往行為良好減刑1/3 二代美國隊長可出獄
(Article 23 Sees First Enforcement: National Security Prisoner Not Granted Early Release Under Previous One-Third Sentence Reduction for Good Behaviour, “Second-Generation Captain America” Could Have Been Freed)
fields.html:
23條首執行 國安囚犯未提早獲釋 倘按過往行為良好減刑1/3 二代美國隊長可出獄

(Article 23 Sees First Enforcement: National Security Prisoner Not Granted Early Release Under Previous One-Third Sentence Reduction for Good Behaviour, “Second-Generation Captain America” Could Have Been Freed)

fields.label: Source
fields.text: 明報 Ming Pao (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)
fields.html: 明報 Ming Pao (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This report examines the first application of Article 23-related measures affecting prisoners convicted of national security offences in Hong Kong. It highlights that such prisoners are no longer eligible for the standard one-third sentence reduction for good behaviour that is ordinarily granted to other inmates. Instead, they must satisfy an additional requirement of demonstrating that they will “not be detrimental to national security” in order to be considered for early release. The report further notes that this requirement has been applied retrospectively, affecting individuals already sentenced under the previous legal framework. As a result, prisoners who would otherwise have qualified for early release – such as the activist known as “Second-Generation Captain America” – remain incarcerated.

It highlights that such prisoners are no longer eligible for the standard one-third sentence reduction for good behaviour that is ordinarily granted to other inmates. Instead, they must satisfy an additional requirement of demonstrating that they will “not be detrimental to national security” in order to be considered for early release. The report further notes that this requirement has been applied retrospectively, affecting individuals already sentenced under the previous legal framework. As a result, prisoners who would otherwise have qualified for early release – such as the activist known as “Second-Generation Captain America” – remain incarcerated.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text:
This exhibit demonstrates the differential and discriminatory treatment of individuals convicted of national security offences, including the denial of sentence reductions routinely available to other prisoners. The imposition of vague and subjective criteria–such as proving one will not endanger national security–introduces arbitrary decision-making and effectively prolongs detention. The retrospective application of these measures further underscores a departure from fundamental principles of legality and non-retroactivity.
This evidence is relevant to establishing persecution and severe deprivation of liberty on political grounds under Article 7 of the Rome Statute, as well as illustrating additional punitive measures imposed specifically on political prisoners, reinforcing the existence of a systematic policy of repression targeting dissenting individuals.

heading: EXHIBIT E27

fields.label: Title
fields.text: HKSAR v Lee Cheuk Yan and Others (HCCC 155/2022) – Press Summary
fields.html: HKSAR v Lee Cheuk Yan and Others (HCCC 155/2022) – Press Summary

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Judiciary of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (Legal Reference System)
fields.html: Judiciary of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (Legal Reference System)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This is the Judiciary's press summary of the judgment of a panel of three designated national-security judges (Alex Lee Wan-tang, Johnny Chan Jong-herng and Anna Lai Yuen-kee) in the prosecution of the former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China. It records that Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung were convicted of incitement to subvert State power and that Albert Ho Chun-yan had pleaded guilty; that the court adopted a starting point of seven years and six months' imprisonment; and that Chow Hang-tung was sentenced to seven years and three months, Lee Cheuk-yan to seven years and Albert Ho to five years and two months, with the Alliance fined HK$1.5 million.

It records that Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung were convicted of incitement to subvert State power and that Albert Ho Chun-yan had pleaded guilty; that the court adopted a starting point of seven years and six months' imprisonment; and that Chow Hang-tung was sentenced to seven years and three months, Lee Cheuk-yan to seven years and Albert Ho to five years and two months, with the Alliance fined HK$1.5 million.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: An official summary, issued by the Judiciary itself, of the outcome and principal reasoning of the case. It establishes, from a source the authorities cannot dispute, the identity of the judges, the conviction of the leaders of the organisation that for three decades organised the commemoration of those killed on 4 June 1989, and the sentences of up to seven years and three months' imprisonment. Relevant to imprisonment under Article 7(1)(e) and persecution on political grounds under Article 7(1)(h).

fields.text: Judiciary of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (Legal Reference System)
fields.html: Judiciary of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (Legal Reference System)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This is the full judgment of the Hong Kong Alliance Case. The court accepted that the case involved no violence or threat of violence and that the defendants had proposed no specific means of implementation or timetable, but held the offence to be of a serious nature, relying on the dissemination of the Alliance's programme to end one-party rule through its organised activities, its Tiananmen commemorations and its social-media presence, and on the defendants' refusal to abandon that position after the HKNSL came into force.

heading: EXHIBIT E29

fields.label: Title
fields.text: HKSAR v WONG CHI-FUNG (黃之鋒) – Reasons for Sentence
fields.html: HKSAR v WONG CHI-FUNG (黃之鋒) – Reasons for Sentence

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Judiciary of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (Legal Reference System)
fields.html: Judiciary of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (Legal Reference System)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This judgment sets out the reasons for sentencing Joshua Wong Chi-fung for conspiracy to commit collusion with foreign countries or with external elements to endanger national security under Article 29 of the HKNSL. The court treated his conduct before the HKNSL as context only. For the period charged, 1 July to 23 November 2020, it relied mainly on his sharing of Nathan Law's Facebook posts and online petition, together with articles and interviews in foreign media. The court held the offence to be "of a grave nature" and took a starting point of 13 years. After allowing for his guilty plea, it imposed the minimum term of 10 years' imprisonment. Only 2 months and 2 days of that term run concurrently with his sentence in the Hong Kong 47 case, from which he was due for release on 7 January 2027.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This judgment shows that sharing social-media posts and publishing commentary in support of advocacy abroad was punished with ten years' imprisonment, imposed on a prisoner who had been in custody since November 2020. It also shows the "collusion" offence being applied to political speech, as in EXHIBIT E10. Relevant to imprisonment under Article 7(1)(e) and persecution under Article 7(1)(h) of the Rome Statute, and to the individual responsibility of TAM Yiu-ho, William.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: In this press release, Chief Executive John Lee responds to Wong's sentencing. He describes Wong Chi-fung, Law Kwun-chung and their accomplices as "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability", and says they "fuelled the 'black-clad violence' and the Hong Kong version of 'colour revolution' in 2019". A Government spokesman states that the Government "will forfeit Wong Chi-fung's offence-related property". The spokesman also says the sentence "completely shattered the illusion" that people endangering national security can escape liability under the guise of "international advocacy".

heading: EXHIBIT F1

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Persons wanted for alleged contravention of Hong Kong National Security Law
fields.html: Persons wanted for alleged contravention of Hong Kong National Security Law

fields.label: Source
fields.text: National Security Department, Hong Kong Police Force (info.gov.hk)
fields.html: National Security Department, Hong Kong Police Force (info.gov.hk)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This press release announces that the court had issued arrest warrants against eight persons who had absconded overseas, alleged to have committed offences under the Hong Kong National Security Law, and offered a reward of HK$1,000,000 in respect of each of them. Three of the eight – Christopher Mung (Mung Siu-tat), Finn Lau (Lau Cho-dik) and Nathan Law (Law Kwun-chung) – are resident in the United Kingdom. The release warns that providing pecuniary or other financial assistance to such persons is itself unlawful, and asserts extraterritorial application of the Law under Articles 37 and 38.

Three of the eight – Christopher Mung (Mung Siu-tat), Finn Lau (Lau Cho-dik) and Nathan Law (Law Kwun-chung) – are resident in the United Kingdom. The release warns that providing pecuniary or other financial assistance to such persons is itself unlawful, and asserts extraterritorial application of the Law under Articles 37 and 38.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: This is the originating instrument of the bounty-and-pursuit programme directed at persons resident in States Parties. It establishes that named individuals resident in the United Kingdom were, from July 2023, made the objects of arrest warrants and public bounties by reason of their political activity in exile, and that the scheme was, from inception, designed to reach persons and their supporters outside Hong Kong. Relevant to persecution under Article 7(1)(h) of the Rome Statute, and to the jurisdiction of the ICC under Article 12(2)(a) of the Rome Statute, the scheme being directed at persons on the territory of a State Party.

title: Persons wanted for alleged contravention of Hong Kong National Security Law
source: National Security Department, Hong Kong Police Force (info.gov.hk)
summary: This press release announces that the court had issued arrest warrants against eight persons who had absconded overseas, alleged to have committed offences under the Hong Kong National Security Law, and offered a reward of HK$1,000,000 in respect of each of them. Three of the eight – Christopher Mung (Mung Siu-tat), Finn Lau (Lau Cho-dik) and Nathan Law (Law Kwun-chung) – are resident in the United Kingdom. The release warns that providing pecuniary or other financial assistance to such persons is itself unlawful, and asserts extraterritorial application of the Law under Articles 37 and 38.
relevance: This is the originating instrument of the bounty-and-pursuit programme directed at persons resident in States Parties. It establishes that named individuals resident in the United Kingdom were, from July 2023, made the objects of arrest warrants and public bounties by reason of their political activity in exile, and that the scheme was, from inception, designed to reach persons and their supporters outside Hong Kong. Relevant to persecution under Article 7(1)(h) of the Rome Statute, and to the jurisdiction of the ICC under Article 12(2)(a) of the Rome Statute, the scheme being directed at persons on the territory of a State Party.

(Chief Executive's Remarks Before Executive Council Meeting and Media Q&A (with video))

fields.label: Source
fields.html: info.gov.hk (Hong Kong Government Press-release Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official press release records the remarks of the Chief Executive, John Lee (Lee Ka-chiu), on 4 July 2023, the day after the wanted notice at EXHIBIT F1. Lee stated that he “fully support[ed] and endorse[d]” the action; that “no matter where they flee to, however far, we will pursue these criminals for life”; that unless they surrendered the wanted persons would remain “living in fear every day, in dread of arrest”; that eligibility for the reward extended to “the relatives and friends of the wanted persons”; and that the authorities would “continue to monitor the conduct of the wanted persons”.

(Secretary for Security speaks on National Security Department's lawful actions to put persons at large on wanted list)

fields.label: Source
fields.html: info.gov.hk (Hong Kong Government Press-release Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official press release records the remarks of the Secretary for Security, Chris Tang (Tang Ping-keung), on 4 July 2023. Tang stated that the wanted persons, having “run off” overseas, “must be severely punished”; that the authorities would “identify their contacts, associates, and the financiers behind them in Hong Kong or overseas”; that “the law enforcement authorities of Hong Kong will devote their whole lives to bringing you back for arrest”; and that a wanted person retaining “use value” to a foreign power would, once that value was lost, “become a discarded pawn”. With specific reference to Nathan Law, Tang described him as a “modern-day traitor of the Chinese nation” and called upon him to surrender.

(Chris Tang: We will devote our entire lives to arresting wanted fugitives)
source: Hong Kong China News Agency (State Media of the People’s Republic of China)
type: Video recording (secondary report of the remarks at EXHIBIT F8)
summary: A video, published by the Hong Kong China News Agency, of the same 4 July 2023 media session, carrying the Secretary for Security’s statements that persons who had “gone overseas” “must be severely punished”, that each was subject to a HK$1,000,000 reward intended to elicit information from persons “whether in Hong Kong or overseas, or anyone connected to these people”, and that such persons would become “a discarded pawn”.
relevance: Corroborates the remarks at EXHIBIT F8 and their dissemination by state media of the People’s Republic of China. Relevant to the policy element and to attribution.

fields.label: Source

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official press release records the remarks of the Chief Executive on 11 July 2023, in which, in response to a question on the pursuit of the eight wanted persons, he stated that “this pursuit will be lifelong, and we will use every possible means to pursue them”, including “holding accountable any person who provides them with financial assistance or other forms of assistance”, and “those providing backing behind them, or even those who may be controlling them”; that “everyone should also regard them as ‘rats crossing the street’, to be shunned”; and that the authorities would “broaden [their] intelligence-gathering and striking network”.

(Full Transcript of Remarks by the Secretary for Security Before His Departure for Vietnam (Chinese Only))

保安局局長啓程往越南前會見傳媒談話全文（只有中文）

(Full Transcript of Remarks by the Secretary for Security Before His Departure for Vietnam (Chinese Only))

fields.label: Source
fields.html: info.gov.hk (Hong Kong Government Press-release Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official press release records remarks of the Secretary for Security on 27 August 2023. Referring to the eight wanted persons, “including Hui Chi-fung and Nathan Law”, he stated that “people must under no circumstances contact them and must guard against them”, and that assisting them could contravene Hong Kong law. Asked about a statement by the United States Government that the National Security Department had “harassed the family members of the eight wanted persons”, the Secretary for Security did not deny the underlying allegation, characterising the making of it as an attempt to “demonise” Hong Kong’s enforcement action.

fields.html:
保安局局長談警務處依法通緝涉嫌違反《香港國安法》的竄逃人及黎智英案（只有中文）

(Full Transcript of Remarks by the Secretary for Security on the Police’s Lawful Pursuit of Fugitives Suspected of Violating the Hong Kong National Security Law, and the “Jimmy Lai Case” (Chinese Only))

fields.label: Source
fields.html: info.gov.hk (Hong Kong Government Press-release Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official press release records remarks of the Secretary for Security on 15 December 2023 concerning the five persons newly named as wanted, including Simon Cheng, Fok Ka-chi and Choi Ming-da. He stated that “no matter where you violate the Hong Kong National Security Law, and no matter how long you wait, you remain a wanted person”; that a foreign power protecting them would discard them “once you lose your use value”; that they would remain “unable to see the light like a rat crossing the street”; and that they would “bring shame upon your family and leave them disgraced”. He confirmed that four persons had been arrested in Hong Kong for providing crowdfunded assistance to Ted Hui and Nathan Law.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official press release records a press conference on 24 December 2024 at which the National Security Department placed six further persons on the wanted list, including Carmen Lau, Tony Chung, Kim-wah Chung and Chloe Cheung. In closing remarks the Secretary for Security stated that the targets included persons “unrepentant” in endangering national security who “wantonly collude with external forces”; that “no person who endangers national security should believe that, by being overseas, they can evade criminal responsibility and escape justice”; that the Government “will use every means available”; and that “violations of the law will always be pursued and punished – however far, they will certainly be struck down”.

(Remarks by the Secretary for Security After Attending the Fight Crime Committee Meeting (with video))

fields.label: Source
fields.html: info.gov.hk (Hong Kong Government Press-release Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official press release records remarks of the Secretary for Security on 31 July 2025. In response to a question concerning the United Kingdom’s consideration of restoring extradition arrangements, he stated that a wanted person overseas “may currently believe yourself safe… but we will use every means available to bring you back to Hong Kong to stand trial”, and that such a person, once of no “use value”, would “become a discarded pawn, or even a political bargaining chip”. In answer to a further question concerning contact between the nineteen “Hong Kong Parliament” wanted persons, including Chin Po-fun, and their family members, he stated that the authorities would conduct investigations into any person providing them with funds “whether in Hong Kong or elsewhere”.

fields.label: Source
fields.text: Hong Kong Commercial Daily (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)
fields.html: Hong Kong Commercial Daily (Hong Kong Local Media Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: A December 2021 interview with the Secretary for Security, in which he stated that ordinary channels of inter-State legal cooperation had been “temporarily suspended” for political reasons; that the only beneficiaries were persons who had “broke[n] the law in Hong Kong, fled, and sought protection from foreign countries”; and that Hong Kong “will certainly use every possible means to arrest” such persons notwithstanding that it could not “extradite them back immediately”.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: Evidence that, from an early stage, the Secretary for Security understood the programme subsequently implemented as a means of achieving, through means other than extradition, the return of persons who had sought protection in foreign States. Relevant to the deliberate and considered character of the programme, and to the assessment of the measures as directed at coercion rather than at any ordinary law-enforcement purpose.

保安局局長談根據《維護國家安全條例》指明危害國家安全罪行的潛逃者及針對他們指明施行的措施
(Remarks by the Secretary for Security on Specifying Absconders Who Have Committed Offences Endangering National Security Under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, and the Measures Specified Against Them)
fields.html:
保安局局長談根據《維護國家安全條例》指明危害國家安全罪行的潛逃者及針對他們指明施行的措施

(Remarks by the Secretary for Security on Specifying Absconders Who Have Committed Offences Endangering National Security Under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, and the Measures Specified Against Them)

fields.label: Source
fields.html: info.gov.hk (Hong Kong Government Press-release Outlet)

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official press release records that the Secretary for Security, exercising powers under sections 89(1) and 89(4) of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, specified six persons – Nathan Law, Christopher Mung, Finn Lau, Simon Cheng, Fok Ka-chi and Choi Ming-da – as “specified absconders”, and imposed measures including prohibitions on providing or dealing with funds, on property dealings, and on joint ventures, together with cancellation of HKSAR passports, suspension of professional qualifications, and removal from directorships, on penalty of up to seven years’ imprisonment. He stated that the six were selected because they were “hiding in the United Kingdom”, and expressly linked the action to the United Kingdom’s prosecution of an employee of the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London. He confirmed that “any person” directly or indirectly providing funds to a specified absconder would be in violation of the law.

fields.label: Relevance
fields.text: Primary evidence of the imposition, by the Secretary for Security personally, of comprehensive financial and civil disability upon named persons resident in a State Party, and of the criminalisation of any person, without geographic limitation, who provides them with financial support. Relevant to persecution under Article 7(1)(h); to other inhumane acts under Article 7(1)(k); to jurisdiction under Article 12(2)(a) of the Rome Statute, the measures being directed at persons and conduct on the territory of a State Party to the Rome Statute; and to the individual responsibility of Chris Tang Ping-keung. The express linkage of the measure to a bilateral dispute with the United Kingdom is further relevant to the character of the conduct as directed at that State Party rather than at the ordinary domestic administration of justice.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: The CPS Initial Details of the Prosecution Case concerning three men charged in connection with foreign-intelligence activity in the United Kingdom. It sets out that Chung Biu Yuen, office manager of the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London, tasked Chi Leung Wai – a serving United Kingdom Border Force officer – to conduct surveillance and information-gathering, and records, among other matters, a surveillance-tasking note dated 16 August 2023 naming Finn Lau and Christopher Mung as subjects, shortly after the July 2023 bounties, together with payments of £95,500 from an HKETO bank account to Wai’s company between June 2023 and January 2024.

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: Reports the opening of the trial of Chung Biu Yuen and Chi Leung Wai at the Central Criminal Court on charges of assisting a foreign intelligence service. heading: EXHIBIT F31

fields.label: Title
fields.text: Two men convicted of National Security Act offences
fields.html: Two men convicted of National Security Act offences

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This official statement reports that Chi Leung Wai and Chung Biu Yuen were found guilty of assisting a foreign intelligence service contrary to the National Security Act 2023, with Wai additionally convicted of misconduct in public office for misuse of Home Office systems. It records that requests originating from Hong Kong were passed to Yuen as HKETO office manager and onward-tasked to Wai, and that the investigation involved over 20 terabytes of data.

heading: EXHIBIT F35

fields.text: UPDATED WITH SENTENCE: CPS secures convictions in Hong Kong unlawful surveillance case
fields.html: UPDATED WITH SENTENCE: CPS secures convictions in Hong Kong unlawful surveillance case

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: This CPS press release reports that the two defendants were convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service through unlawful surveillance conducted within the United Kingdom, a State Party to the Rome Statute; that the HKETO was used as a base through which the activities were organised and funded; that the activities included researching UK-resident dissidents and identifying their addresses, vehicles and social-media accounts; and that bounties of up to £100,000 had been issued by Hong Kong authorities. It characterises the conduct as “transnational repression”, “foreign interference”, and “unauthorised surveillance” on British soil.

It characterises the conduct as “transnational repression”, “foreign interference”, and “unauthorised surveillance” on British soil.

heading: EXHIBIT F37

fields.label: Title
fields.text: R v Chung Biu (Bill) Yuen and Chi Leung (Peter) Wai – Sentencing Remarks
fields.html: R v Chung Biu (Bill) Yuen and Chi Leung (Peter) Wai – Sentencing Remarks

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: The sentencing remarks following the conviction of the two men. The remarks record, at paragraph 29, that Wai’s misuse of the Home Office database extended to surveillance of Nathan Law while Law was speaking at a public event at the Oxford Union, and that Wai testified that he believed activists such as Law deserved to be described as “cockroaches” – language the judge described as dehumanising terminology used by the Chinese regime toward pro-democracy protesters. The remarks record that Yuen, HKETO’s office manager, acted as the “conduit, organiser and facilitator” through whom requests from Hong Kong were received and transmitted, and describe the conduct as “shadow policing operations”.

fields.html: HKSAR Government disapproves of and opposes untrue and biased remarks by UK

fields.label: Summary
fields.text: Issued the day after the joint statement of the United Kingdom’s Foreign Secretary and Home Secretary (EXHIBIT F38), this press release names both Secretaries of State, characterises their remarks as “untrue and biased”, and reaffirms the programme: it asserts that “those absconders hiding in the UK and other Western countries are wanted because they continue to blatantly engage in activities endangering national security”; that “any individuals who endanger national security should not believe that being outside Hong Kong will allow them to evade criminal responsibility”; that the Government “will exhaust all means to pursue and combat” such persons “regardless of the distance”; and demands that the United Kingdom “immediately stop interfering in Hong Kong matters”.
